Spanish Oil & Gas Services Sector Recalled to 2017 Debt Crisis as Industry Recovers

Madrid—Industry experts are reflecting on the severe debt crisis that swept through Spain’s Oil & Gas Services & Equipment sector in 2017, sending shockwaves through the industry and reshaping its financial landscape. 

The crisis originated in the spring of 2017 when a sudden and sustained collapse in global oil prices—dropping Brent crude below $40 per barrel—coincided with a tightening of credit conditions across Spanish banks. As a result, many mid-sized and smaller oilfield services firms, including Driltek Iberia and ServiPetro S.L., found themselves unable to service existing debts or secure new financing.

Within weeks, the Spanish Association of Oil & Gas Services (ASESP) warned of “unprecedented liquidity pressures” in an industry already grappling with reduced exploration budgets from upstream clients. “We were hit from both sides: clients slashed spending, and the banks closed their doors. Some companies had days, not weeks, to find cash,” recalled Javier Escudero, ASESP’s secretary general.

By mid-2017, at least eight firms representing more than 30% of the sector’s workforce had filed for bankruptcy protection, according to data from the Ministry of Industry, Energy and Tourism. Unpaid invoices and halted projects became widespread. “In our region, more than 400 skilled jobs were lost in the space of two months,” said Teresa Gómez, spokesperson for the Workers’ Union of Technical Services. “The human cost was immediate and devastating.”

Credit rating agency EuroRisco downgraded the sector to “high risk” in July of that year, citing a “cascade of defaults and rapidly deteriorating asset values.” Equipment suppliers, many of which were heavily leveraged after years of expansion, were forced into fire sales of assets at steep discounts. 

Analysts point to weak balance sheets and overreliance on short-term financing as key factors that left the sector exposed. “Many firms had bet on ongoing high prices and easy credit,” explained Lucas Martín, senior energy analyst at Finansa Research. “When both disappeared, the system unraveled quickly.”

The government’s response included emergency liquidity lines and a temporary deferral of tax payments, which helped stabilize the industry in the latter half of 2017. By 2018, oil prices had partially rebounded and credit conditions improved, allowing surviving firms to restructure debt and resume operations.

While the Spanish Oil & Gas Services & Equipment sector has since returned to stability, the scars from the 2017 debt crisis remain a cautionary tale for industry insiders and policymakers alike.
